 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q12a",w:804,h:311,needsHeading:false},svg:svgCube2cm,n:"12(a)",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Volume",marks:2,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"The diagram shows a cube of side length 2 cm.\nVera says, 'The volume of any solid made with 6 of these cubes is 48 cm³'",text:"(a) Is Vera correct?\nYou must show your working.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"Yes — each cube has volume 2×2×2=8 cm³, so 6 cubes always have a total volume of 48 cm³, whatever shape they're arranged into.",markscheme:"M1 for 2×2×2 (=8). C1 for 6×8=48 with the conclusion that volume is unaffected by arrangement, so Vera is correct."},
 {n:"12(b)",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Surface area",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q12b",w:1008,h:321,needsHeading:true},paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(i) For example, a 2 cm × 2 cm × 12 cm cuboid (a single row of 6 cubes) — any arrangement with volume 48 cm³ and whole-cube dimensions is valid. (ii) For a 2×2×12 cm cuboid: 104 cm²",markscheme:"(i) B1 for any valid cuboid arrangement with correctly labelled dimensions that multiply to 48 (e.g. 2×2×12, 2×4×6). (ii) M1 for a correct method to find surface area of their chosen cuboid, e.g. 2(2×2)+4(2×12). A1 ft cao for their cuboid's dimensions."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q13",w:1045,h:119,needsHeading:false},n:"13",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Angles in triangles (algebraic)",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"The size of the largest angle in a triangle is 4 times the size of the smallest angle.\nThe other angle is 27° less than the largest angle.\nWork out, in degrees, the size of each angle in the triangle.\nYou must show your working.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"23°, 92°, 65°",markscheme:"M1 for forming an equation, e.g. s + 4s + (4s−27) = 180. M1 for 9s = 207. A1 for s=23 (smallest). A1 for 4s=92 (largest) and 4s−27=65 (other), all three correctly identified."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q14a",w:812,h:280,needsHeading:false},n:"14(a)",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Currency conversion",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"Andy went on holiday to Canada. His flights cost a total of £1500\nAndy stayed for 14 nights. His hotel room cost $196 per night.\nAndy used wifi for 12 days. Wifi cost $5 per day.\nThe exchange rate was $1.90 to £1",text:"(a) Work out the total cost of the flights, the hotel room and wifi.\nGive your answer in pounds.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"£2975.79 (2 dp)",markscheme:"M1 for 196×14 (=2744, hotel in $). M1 for 5×12 (=60, wifi in $). M1 for (2744+60)÷1.90 (=1475.79, converted to £). A1 for adding £1500. A1 cao. Answer: £2975.79"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q14b",w:889,h:280,needsHeading:false},n:"14(b)",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Currency conversion (reasoning)",marks:1,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"(b) If there were fewer dollars to £1, what effect would this have on the total cost, in pounds, of Andy's holiday?",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"The total cost in pounds would increase (since each £1 would buy fewer dollars, so more pounds are needed to cover the same dollar costs).",markscheme:"C1 for a correct statement that the cost in pounds would increase."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q15",w:800,h:587,needsHeading:false},svg:svgVennAB,n:"15",higherN:"1",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Probability",subtopic:"Venn diagrams",marks:6,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"E = {odd numbers less than 30}\nA = {3, 9, 15, 21, 27}\nB = {5, 15, 25}",text:"(a) Complete the Venn diagram to represent this information.\nA number is chosen at random from the universal set, E.\n(b) What is the probability that the number is in the set A ∪ B?",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(a) A only: 3, 9, 21, 27; both A and B: 15; B only: 5, 25; outside A and B (but in E): 1, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29\n(b) 7/15",markscheme:"(a) B1 for 15 placed in the intersection. B1 for 3,9,21,27 placed in A only. B1 for 5,25 placed in B only. B1 for the remaining 8 elements of E placed outside both circles. (b) M1 for |A∪B|=7. A1 cao. Answer: 7/15"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q16",w:812,h:593,needsHeading:false},n:"16",higherN:"2",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Simultaneous equations",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Solve the simultaneous equations\n3<em>x</em> + <em>y</em> = −4\n3<em>x</em> − 4<em>y</em> = 6",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"x = −2/3, y = −2",markscheme:"M1 for subtracting the equations to eliminate x, giving 5y=−10. A1 for y=−2. A1 (ft) for substituting to find x=−2/3."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q17a",w:747,h:293,needsHeading:false},svg:tblDressSizes,n:"17(a)",higherN:"3(a)",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Averages (median, frequency table)",marks:1,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"The table shows some information about the dress sizes of 25 women.\nDress size 8: 2 women; 10: 9 women; 12: 8 women; 14: 6 women",text:"(a) Find the median dress size.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"12",markscheme:"B1 for identifying the 13th value (median of 25) falls in the 'size 12' group. Answer: 12"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q17b",w:921,h:506,needsHeading:false},n:"17(b)",higherN:"3(b)",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Probability",subtopic:"Mutually exclusive events",marks:1,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"3 of the 25 women have a shoe size of 7\nZoe says that if you choose at random one of the 25 women, the probability that she has either a shoe size of 7 or a dress size of 14 is 9/25 because 3/25 + 6/25 = 9/25\n(b) Is Zoe correct?\nYou must give a reason for your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"Not necessarily — this addition rule only works if the two events are mutually exclusive (no woman has both a shoe size of 7 and a dress size of 14); Zoe hasn't shown this is the case.",markscheme:"C1 for identifying that the events need to be mutually exclusive for the addition rule to be valid, and this hasn't been established."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q18",w:871,h:207,needsHeading:false},n:"18",higherN:"4",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio and fractions/percentages combined",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Daniel bakes 420 cakes.\nHe bakes only vanilla cakes, banana cakes, lemon cakes and chocolate cakes.\n2/7 of the cakes are vanilla cakes.\n35% of the cakes are banana cakes.\nThe ratio of the number of lemon cakes to the number of chocolate cakes is 4 : 5\nWork out the number of lemon cakes Daniel bakes.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"68",markscheme:"M1 for 420×2/7 (=120) vanilla. M1 for 420×0.35 (=147) banana. M1 for 420−120−147 (=153) remaining. M1 for 153×4/9 (=68). A1 cao. Answer: 68"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q19",w:751,h:381,needsHeading:false},svg:svgPolygonPSquares,n:"19",higherN:"5",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Polygons and interior angles",marks:4,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"In the diagram, AB, BC and CD are three sides of a regular polygon P. At A there is a square, at D there is a square, and at E (below B and C) there is a regular 12-sided polygon, all sharing sides with polygon P.",text:"Show that polygon P is a hexagon.\nYou must show your working.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"Interior angle of a square = 90°. Interior angle of a regular 12-gon = 150°. At vertex B, the angles around the point sum to 360°: 90° + (interior angle of P) + 150° = 360°, so the interior angle of P = 120°. The same applies at C. A polygon with interior angle 120° is a regular hexagon (interior angle = (n−2)×180/n = 120 gives n=6).",markscheme:"M1 for interior angle of a regular 12-sided polygon = 150°. M1 for using angles around a point = 360° to find the interior angle of P (=120°). A1 for using (n−2)×180/n=120 or equivalent. C1 for concluding n=6, so P is a hexagon."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3FH-Q20",w:1045,h:221,needsHeading:false},n:"20",higherN:"6",tier:"Crossover",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Density and compound measures",marks:4,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"The density of apple juice is 1.05 grams per cm³.\nThe density of fruit syrup is 1.4 grams per cm³.\nThe density of carbonated water is 0.99 grams per cm³.\n25 cm³ of apple juice are mixed with 15 cm³ of fruit syrup and 280 cm³ of carbonated water to make a drink with a volume of 320 cm³.\nWork out the density of the drink.\nGive your answer correct to 2 decimal places.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"1.01 g/cm³",markscheme:"M1 for 25×1.05 (=26.25), 15×1.4 (=21), 280×0.99 (=277.2) — mass of each component. M1 for total mass (=324.45 g). A1 for 324.45÷320. A1 cao to 2 dp. Answer: 1.01 g/cm³"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3F-Q21",w:875,h:281,needsHeading:false},svg:svgSimilarTriangles345,n:"21",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Similar shapes (Pythagorean triples)",marks:2,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"Two right-angled triangles are shown: one with sides 7.5 cm, 10 cm, 12.5 cm; the other with sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm.",text:"Show that these two triangles are mathematically similar.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"7.5/3 = 10/4 = 12.5/5 = 2.5, so all three corresponding sides are in the same ratio (2.5:1), meaning the triangles are similar.",markscheme:"M1 for calculating at least two of the ratios (7.5÷3, 10÷4, 12.5÷5). C1 for showing all three ratios equal 2.5, with conclusion that the triangles are similar."},

 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q8",w:669,h:149,needsHeading:false},svg:svgSquareInCircle,n:"H8",tier:"Higher",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Circles and Pythagoras",marks:4,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"A square, with sides of length x cm, is inside a circle. Each vertex of the square is on the circumference of the circle. The area of the circle is 49 cm².",text:"Work out the value of x.\nGive your answer correct to 3 significant figures.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"5.59 cm",markscheme:"M1 for finding the radius from πr²=49 (r≈3.9493). M1 for recognising the diagonal of the square equals the diameter (2r≈7.8987). M1 for x = diagonal/√2. A1 cao to 3 sf. Answer: 5.59 cm"},
 {n:"H9",tier:"Higher",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Box plots",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q9",w:998,h:965,needsHeading:false},paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(a) £180 (b) A box plot with whiskers from 60 to 650, box from 180 to 350, and median line at 300. (c) Not necessarily — the female students' median (£300) is higher, but box plots only summarise the distribution (medians and quartiles); we can't conclude every individual female student spent more than every male student.",markscheme:"(a) M1 for evidence of using the lower quartile (£150) and upper quartile (£330), e.g. 330 − 150. A1 cao. Answer: £180 (b) M1 for the box drawn from 180 to 350 with the median marked at 300. A1 for whiskers correctly drawn to 60 and 650. (c) C1 for a correct comparison, e.g. the female median/quartiles being higher shows the female group tended to spend more on average, but this doesn't mean every female spent more than every male."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q10",w:620,h:121,needsHeading:false},n:"H10",tier:"Higher",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Compound interest (reverse)",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Naoby invests £6000 for 5 years.\nThe investment gets compound interest of x% per annum.\nAt the end of 5 years the investment is worth £8029.35\nWork out the value of x.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"x = 6",markscheme:"M1 for setting up 6000×(1+x/100)⁵=8029.35. M1 for (8029.35/6000)^(1/5). A1 cao. Answer: x = 6"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q11",w:850,h:189,needsHeading:false},n:"H11",tier:"Higher",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Product rule for counting",marks:2,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Jeff is choosing a shrub and a rose tree for his garden.\nAt the garden centre there are 17 different types of shrubs and some rose trees.\nJeff says, 'There are 215 different ways to choose one shrub and one rose tree.'\nCould Jeff be correct?\nYou must show how you get your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"No — 215 ÷ 17 = 12.6 (not a whole number), but the number of rose trees must be a whole number, so Jeff cannot be correct.",markscheme:"M1 for 215÷17. C1 for concluding No, since 12.6 is not a whole number."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q12",w:929,h:115,needsHeading:false},svg:svgPointsOnLine,n:"H12",tier:"Higher",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Ratio on a line (algebraic)",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"The points A, B, C and D lie in order on a straight line.\nAB : BD = 1 : 5\nAC : CD = 7 : 11\nWork out AB : BC : CD",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"3 : 4 : 11",markscheme:"M1 for expressing AD in two consistent unit systems (AB:BD=1:5 gives AD=6 parts; AC:CD=7:11 gives AD=18 parts, so 1 part of the first system = 3 parts of the second). M1 for AB=3, giving BC=AC−AB=7−3=4 (in the 18-part system) and CD=11. A1 cao. Answer: AB:BC:CD = 3:4:11"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q13",w:958,h:567,needsHeading:false},svg:svgInequalityRegion,n:"H13",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Graphical inequalities",marks:4,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"A graph shows a shaded triangular region bounded by the lines y = 2, y = x and y = 0.5x + 1.",text:"Write down the three inequalities that define the shaded region.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"y ≤ 2, y ≤ x, y ≥ 0.5x + 1",markscheme:"M1 for y = 2 indicated (accept any inequality sign in place of \u2018=\u2019). M1 for y = x indicated. M1 for y = 0.5x + 1 indicated. A1 for y ≤ 2, y ≤ x and y ≥ 0.5x + 1 with the correct inequality signs."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q14a",w:337,h:60,needsHeading:false},n:"H14(a)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Algebraic fractions (factorising)",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"(a) Simplify (<em>x</em>² − 16)/(2<em>x</em>² − 5<em>x</em> − 12)",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(x + 4)/(2x + 3)",markscheme:"M1 for factorising the numerator as (x−4)(x+4). M1 for factorising the denominator as (x−4)(2x+3). A1 cao for cancelling the common factor. Answer: (x+4)/(2x+3)"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q14b",w:550,h:56,needsHeading:true},n:"H14(b)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Rearranging formulae",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"(b) Make v the subject of the formula <em>w</em> = 15(<em>t</em> − 2<em>v</em>)/<em>v</em>",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"v = 15t / (w + 30)",markscheme:"M1 for multiplying both sides by v: wv = 15t − 30v. M1 for collecting v terms: wv + 30v = 15t, i.e. v(w+30)=15t. A1 cao. Answer: v = 15t/(w+30)"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q15",w:772,h:471,needsHeading:false},svg:svgTriangle45,n:"H15",tier:"Higher",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Trigonometry (area of triangle)",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"In triangle ABC, AB = (2x − 1) metres, AC = (x + 3) metres, and angle ABC = 45°.\nThe area of triangle ABC is 6√2 m².\nCalculate the value of x.\nGive your answer correct to 3 significant figures.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"x = 2.63",markscheme:"M1 for Area = ½×(2x−1)×(x+3)×sin45°. M1 for forming the equation ½(2x−1)(x+3)sin45° = 6√2. M1 for rearranging to a quadratic in x. A1 for solving the quadratic. A1 cao to 3 sf. Answer: x = 2.63"},
 {n:"H16",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Iteration",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q16",w:990,h:544,needsHeading:false},paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(a) x₁ = −2.64, x₂ = −2.5739 (4 dp), x₃ = −2.6038 (4 dp) (b) The iteration is converging towards a root of x³ + 2x² + 4 = 0 — as n increases, xₙ gets closer to a solution of that equation (since rearranging x = −2 − 4/x² gives x³ + 2x² + 4 = 0).",markscheme:"(a) M1 for correct substitution of x₀ to find x₁. M1 for correctly iterating to find x₂. A1 for x₃ correct to at least 3 dp (all three values correct). (b) C1 for stating the values are converging to a root of the cubic equation. C1 for showing algebraically that the iteration formula rearranges to give x³+2x²+4=0."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q17a",w:822,h:149,needsHeading:false},n:"H17(a)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Bounds (compound measures)",marks:4,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"A train travelled along a track in 110 minutes, correct to the nearest 5 minutes.\nJake finds out that the track is 270 km long.\nHe assumes that the track has been measured correct to the nearest 10 km.",text:"(a) Could the average speed of the train have been greater than 160 km/h?\nYou must show how you get your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"No — using the bounds (275 km ÷ 107.5 min), the maximum possible average speed is about 153.5 km/h, which is less than 160 km/h.",markscheme:"M1 for identifying the lower time bound (107.5 minutes). M1 for identifying the upper distance bound (275 km, nearest 10 km). M1 for calculating the maximum speed = 275÷(107.5/60). A1 for a correct conclusion (No, since ≈153.5 km/h < 160 km/h)."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q17b",w:591,h:86,needsHeading:true},n:"H17(b)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Bounds (reasoning)",marks:1,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Jake's assumption was wrong. The track was measured correct to the nearest 5 km.\n(b) Explain how this could affect your decision in part (a).",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"With a narrower bound (272.5 km instead of 275 km), the maximum possible average speed is even lower (about 152.1 km/h), so the conclusion in part (a) is unaffected — it's still not possible to exceed 160 km/h.",markscheme:"C1 for recognising the tighter bound reduces the maximum possible distance/speed, so the original 'No' conclusion still holds."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q18",w:1045,h:467,needsHeading:false},svg:svgCircleTangentsD,n:"H18",tier:"Higher",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Arc length and tangents",marks:5,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",intro:"A, B and C are points on a circle of radius 5 cm, centre O. DA and DC are tangents to the circle. DO = 9 cm.",text:"Work out the length of arc ABC.\nGive your answer correct to 3 significant figures.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"21.6 cm",markscheme:"M1 for recognising angle OAD = 90° (tangent perpendicular to radius). M1 for angle AOD = arccos(5/9) (≈56.25°). M1 for the reflex angle AOC (major arc side) = 360 − 2×56.25° (≈247.5°). M1 for arc length = (247.5/360)×2π×5. A1 cao to 3 sf. Answer: 21.6 cm"},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q19",w:283,h:24,needsHeading:false},n:"H19",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Quadratic inequalities",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"Solve 2<em>x</em>² + 3<em>x</em> − 2 > 0",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"x < −2 or x > 1/2",markscheme:"M1 for factorising 2x²+3x−2 as (2x−1)(x+2). A1 for critical values x=1/2 and x=−2. A1 for correct inequality x<−2 or x>1/2 (not an 'and' statement)."},
 {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q20a",w:1045,h:91,needsHeading:false},n:"H20(a)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Exponential graphs",marks:1,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"The equation of a curve is <em>y</em> = <em>a</em><span class=\"exp\"><em>x</em></span>\n<em>A</em> is the point where the curve intersects the <em>y</em>-axis.\n(a) State the coordinates of <em>A</em>.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"(0, 1)",markscheme:"B1 cao.  {qimg:{src:"Sum2017-3H-Q20b",w:613,h:215,needsHeading:true},svg:svgCircleTranslated,n:"H20(b)",tier:"Higher",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Circle equations and translations",marks:3,paperNum:"3",sitting:"Summer 2017",text:"The equation of circle C is <em>x</em>² + <em>y</em>² = 16\nThe circle C is translated by the vector (3, 0) to give circle B.\n(b) Draw a sketch of circle B.\nLabel with coordinates the centre of circle B and any points of intersection with the x-axis.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",answer:"Circle B has centre (3, 0) and radius 4 (unchanged by translation). {qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q9",w:510,h:328,needsHeading:false},n:"9",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Written methods and errors",marks:1,text:"Jacqui wants to work out 3480 ÷ 5\nShe knows that 3480 ÷ 10 = 348\nJacqui writes\n3480 ÷ 5 = 174\nbecause 10 ÷ 5 = 2 and 348 ÷ 2 = 174\nWhat mistake did Jacqui make in her method?",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"She divided 348 by 2 instead of multiplying it by 2 (348 × 2 = 696, not 348 ÷ 2)",markscheme:"C1 for identifying the error in the method, e.g. she should have multiplied 348 by 2, not divided."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q10",w:959,h:800,needsHeading:false},n:"10",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Comparing data sets",marks:2,text:"Jake and Sarah each played a computer game six times.\nTheir scores for each game are shown in the table.\n(a) Who had the most consistent scores, Jake or Sarah? (b) C1 for a valid reason, e.g. the stem was not used, or it should be 26."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q11",w:671,h:325,needsHeading:false},n:"11",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:3,text:"There are 30 children in a nursery school.\nAt least 1 adult is needed for every 8 children in the nursery.\n(a) Work out the least number of adults needed in the nursery.\n2 more children join the nursery.\n(b) Does this mean that more adults are needed in the nursery? You must give a reason for your answer.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 4  (b) No, with reason (32 children still only need 4 adults since 4 × 8 = 32)",markscheme:"(a) P1 for 30 ÷ 8, or 3.75, or 3, or counting up in 8s towards 30 to at least 3 lots of 8, or 4 × 8 (=32) oe. {qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q15",w:1045,h:114,needsHeading:false},n:"15",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio and percentages combined",marks:2,text:"There are only red buttons, yellow buttons and orange buttons in a jar.\nThe number of red buttons, the number of yellow buttons and the number of orange buttons are in the ratio 7 : 4 : 9\nWork out what percentage of the buttons in the jar are orange.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"45%",markscheme:"M1 for a correct first step, e.g. 9/(7+4+9) (=9/20), or 100/(7+4+9) (=5), or a full method for one of the other colours. A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q16",w:872,h:477,needsHeading:false},n:"16",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Percentage decrease (discounts)",marks:5,text:"Berenika wants to buy 35 T-shirts.\nEach T-shirt costs £5.80\nBerenika does the calculation 40 × 6 = 240 to estimate the cost of 35 T-shirts.\n(a) Explain how Berenika’s calculation shows the actual cost will be less than £240\nThere is a special offer.\nT-shirts £5.80 each. Buy 30 or more T-shirts. Get 10% off the total cost.\n(b) Work out the actual cost of buying 35 T-shirts using the special offer.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) Both 40 and 6 were rounded up from 35 and 5.80, so 240 is an overestimate  (b) £182.70",markscheme:"(a) C1 for an explanation, e.g. states both values were over-estimated. (b) P1 for a process to find 10% of a value in the question. P1 for a process to find 90% of a value in the question. P1 for a complete process to find the actual cost of 35. A1 cao (SC B2 for 156.60)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q17",w:758,h:399,needsHeading:false},n:"17",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Probability",subtopic:"Combined events",marks:2,text:"There are 3 cards in Box A and 3 cards in Box B. There is a number on each card.\nRyan takes at random a card from Box A and a card from Box B.\nHe adds together the numbers on the two cards to get a total score.\nWork out the probability that the total score is an odd number.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"4/9",markscheme:"M1 for listed outcomes (allow 1 error, e.g. omission or repeat), or fractions 1/3×2/3 + 2/3×1/3. A1 for 4/9 oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q18",w:815,h:63,needsHeading:false},n:"18",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:2,text:"Harry, Regan and Kelan share £450 in the ratio 2 : 5 : 3\nHow much money does Kelan get?",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"£135",markscheme:"M1 for 450 ÷ (2+3+5) (=45), or 3/10 × 450 (=135), or 5 parts are 225, or 2 parts are 90. A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q19",w:1045,h:298,needsHeading:false},n:"19",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Direct and inverse proportion",marks:3,text:"Here is a list of ingredients for making 16 flapjacks.\nIngredients for 16 flapjacks: 120 g butter, 140 g brown sugar, 250 g oats, 2 tablespoons syrup\nJenny wants to make 24 flapjacks.\nWork out how much of each of the ingredients she needs.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"180 g butter, 210 g brown sugar, 375 g oats, 3 tablespoons syrup",markscheme:"M1 for 24/16 (=1.5), or 16/24 oe, or 0.5 of any figure in the recipe calculated, or the amount of any ingredient for 1 flapjack, or 3 tablespoons found. M1 for a method to scale at least one ingredient in grams, e.g. 120 × 1.5, 140 × 1.5 or 250 × 1.5. A1 for all quantities correct."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q20",w:621,h:178,needsHeading:false},n:"20",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Estimation (checking calculations)",marks:3,text:"Ami and Josh use a calculator to work out <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">595</span><span class=\"den\">4.08² + 5.3</span></span>\nAmi’s answer is 27.1115\nJosh’s answer is 271.115\nOne of these answers is correct.\nUse approximations to find out which answer is correct.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Ami’s answer (27.1115) is correct",markscheme:"M2 for an approximate calculation, e.g. 600/(16+5), 600/21, 600/20 or 600/25 oe (M1 for using 600, 5 or 4 in an approximation). C1 for concluding Ami’s answer is closest, with an accurately calculated approximate figure shown."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q21",w:405,h:91,needsHeading:false},n:"21",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Standard form",marks:3,text:"Work out <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">0.06 &times; 0.0003</span><span class=\"den\">0.01</span></span>\nGive your answer in standard form.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"1.8 &times; 10<span class=\"exp\">−3</span>",markscheme:"M2 for (6×10⁻²×3×10⁻⁴)/(1×10⁻²), or 18×10⁻⁴, or 0.0018 as the answer (M1 for 6 × 0.0003, or 0.06 × 0.03, or 1.8 × 10ⁿ where n ≠ −3, or 0.000018 ÷ 0.01, or rewriting one number in standard form). A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q22",w:367,h:343,needsHeading:false},n:"22",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Adding and subtracting fractions",marks:3,text:"(a) Work out <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">2</span><span class=\"den\">5</span></span> + <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1</span><span class=\"den\">4</span></span>\n(b) Write down the value of 2<span class=\"exp\">−3</span>",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 13/20  (b) 1/8",markscheme:"(a) M1 for a suitable common denominator with one fraction correct, or 0.4 + 0.25. A1 for 13/20 or 0.65 oe. (b) B1 for 1/8, accept 0.125."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q23",w:466,h:28,needsHeading:false},n:"23",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Prime factorisation",marks:2,text:"Write 36 as a product of its prime factors.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"2 &times; 2 &times; 3 &times; 3",markscheme:"M1 for a complete method to find the prime factors, which could be shown on a complete factor tree with no more than one arithmetic error, or 2, 2, 3, 3. A1 for 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q24",w:624,h:119,needsHeading:false},n:"24",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:4,text:"Kiaria is 7 years older than Jay.\nMartha is twice as old as Kiaria.\nThe sum of their three ages is 77\nFind the ratio of Jay’s age to Kiaria’s age to Martha’s age.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"14 : 21 : 42",markscheme:"P1 for 2 of the 3 expressions in one letter, e.g. x, x+7, 2x+14, or a set of numbers showing interpretation of the relationships, e.g. 10, 17, 34. P1 (dep) for the sum of the three expressions = 77, e.g. x + x+7 + 2x+14 = 77 oe, or two systematic correct trials including addition. P1 for a correct process to isolate the term in x, or x = 14. A1 for the ratio 14 : 21 : 42 oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q25",w:809,h:561,needsHeading:false},n:"25",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Geometric proof",marks:4,text:"<em>ABCD</em> is a parallelogram.\n<em>EDC</em> is a straight line.\n<em>F</em> is the point on <em>AD</em> so that <em>BFE</em> is a straight line.\nAngle <em>EFD</em> = 35°\nAngle <em>DCB</em> = 75°\nShow that angle <em>ABF</em> = 70°\nGive a reason for each stage of your working.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Angle ABF = 70° (shown, with reasons)",markscheme:"B1 for identifying 35°, 75°, 145° or 105°, or angle DEF = 70°, marked on the diagram, or a 3-letter description. M1 for 180−70−35 or 180−75−35, or a correct pair of angles that would lead to 75° or 70° (e.g. angle AFB = 35° and angle FAB = 75°). C2 (dep on B1, M1) for all figures correct with all appropriate reasons stated and clearly labelled (C1 dep for one reason clearly used and stated). Reasons may include: corresponding angles are equal; alternate angles are equal; opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal; angles in a triangle sum to 180°; angles on a straight line sum to 180°; co-interior (allied) angles sum to 180°."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q26",w:747,h:621,needsHeading:false},n:"26",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Area of a circle and estimation",marks:4,text:"The diagram shows a logo made from three circles.\nEach circle has centre <em>O</em>.\nDaisy says that exactly <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1</span><span class=\"den\">3</span></span> of the logo is shaded.\nIs Daisy correct?\nYou must show all your working.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"No, Daisy is not correct (the shaded fraction is 33/100, not 1/3)",markscheme:"P1 for a process to find the area of any relevant circle, i.e. π×4² (=16π), π×7² (=49π), π×10² (=100π), or 7² and 4². P1 (supported) for a completed method to find the shaded area, e.g. \"π×7²\" − \"π×4²\" (=33π), or use of radii, e.g. 7² − 4² (=33). A1 for two comparable figures, e.g. 33π and 100π, or 33 and 100. C1 for a statement, e.g. no because it should be 33/100, supported by their accurate figures."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q27",w:930,h:835,needsHeading:false},n:"27",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Averages (mean)",marks:4,text:"The table shows information about the weekly earnings of 20 people who work in a shop.\n(a) Work out an estimate for the mean of the weekly earnings.\nNadiya says, “The mean may not be the best average to use to represent this information.”\n(b) Do you agree with Nadiya? You must justify your answer.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) £365  (b) Agree, with reason (the highest interval is an outlier that pulls the mean up)",markscheme:"(a) M1 for fx with x consistent within intervals, e.g. 200×1, 300×11, 400×5, 500×0, 600×3 (condone 1 error if figures given without working). M1 (dep) for Σfx ÷ Σf, e.g. \"7300\" ÷ 20. A1 cao. (b) C1 for a comment about outliers affecting the mean."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q28",w:737,h:544,needsHeading:false},n:"28",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Forming and showing equations",marks:4,text:"Here is a rectangle.\nAll measurements are in centimetres.\nThe area of the rectangle is 48 cm².\nShow that <em>y</em> = 3",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"y = 3 (shown)",markscheme:"M1 for forming an equation, e.g. 2x + 6 = 5x − 9. M1 for isolating x and number terms, e.g. 3x = 15. M1 for substituting x = 5 into a side length, e.g. 2×5 + 6 (=16). A1 for 48 ÷ 16 = 3, showing y = 3."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q29",w:845,h:740,needsHeading:false},n:"29",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Graphs of quadratic functions",marks:1,text:"Brogan needs to draw the graph of <em>y</em> = <em>x</em>² + 1\nHere is her graph.\nWrite down one thing that is wrong with Brogan’s graph.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"The graph should be a smooth curve, not straight line segments",markscheme:"B1 for a correct mathematical comment, e.g. line segments not a curve, or it should be drawn freehand rather than with a ruler. (Comments about scale or plotting accuracy are not accepted.)"},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-1F-Q30",w:815,h:91,needsHeading:false},n:"30",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Reverse percentages",marks:2,text:"In a sale, the normal price of a book is reduced by 30%.\nThe sale price of the book is £2.80\nWork out the normal price of the book.",paper:"Paper 1 (non-calculator)",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"£4",markscheme:"M1 for a complete method, e.g. 2.80 × 100 ÷ (100−30) oe, or 2.80 ÷ 0.7 oe (or a build-up method showing all intermediate steps unless all figures are correct, e.g. 2.8 ÷ 7 = 0.4 and \"0.40\" × 10 = 4). A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q1",w:298,h:60,needsHeading:false},n:"1",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"FDP conversions",marks:1,text:"Write <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">7</span><span class=\"den\">100</span></span> as a decimal.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"0.07",markscheme:"B1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q2",w:578,h:28,needsHeading:false},n:"2",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Multiples and factors",marks:1,text:"Write down a multiple of 6 that is between 40 and 50",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"42 or 48",markscheme:"B1 for 42 or 48."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q3",w:278,h:368,needsHeading:false},n:"3",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Simplifying and collecting terms",marks:3,text:"(a) Simplify 3<em>f</em> × 5<em>g</em>\n(b) Simplify <em>t</em> × <em>t</em>\n(c) Simplify <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">2<em>n</em> + 6<em>n</em></span><span class=\"den\">2</span></span>",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 15fg  (b) t²  (c) 4n",markscheme:"(a) B1 for 15fg. (b) B1 for t². (c) B1 for 4n."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q4",w:743,h:901,needsHeading:false},n:"4",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Calculations with measures",marks:6,text:"Ken buys some fruit. He buys apples, bananas, peaches and oranges.\nKen buys 4 apples weighing 125 g each, 2 bananas weighing 170 g each and 3 peaches weighing 135 g each.\nEach orange has a weight of 90 g.\nThe fruit has a total weight of 1.785 kg.\n(a) Work out how many oranges Ken buys.\nJane wants to buy 15 tomatoes.\nShe asks for 1 kg of tomatoes at a shop.\nJane assumes that each tomato has a weight of 75 g.\n(b) (i) If Jane’s assumption is correct, will she get 15 tomatoes? You must show how you get your answer.\n(ii) If Jane’s assumption is not correct, could she get 15 tomatoes? Justify your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 6 oranges  (b)(i) No  (ii) Yes, she could, if each tomato weighs less than 75 g",markscheme:"(a) P1 for a process to find the total weight of one type of fruit, e.g. 4×125 (=500), 2×170 (=340) or 3×135 (=405). P1 for a complete process to find the total weight of oranges, e.g. 1785−(500+340+405), or sight of 540. A1 cao (SC B1 for 15). (b)(i) P1 for starting the process, e.g. 1000÷75 or 15×75 (=1125). C1 for “No” with correct supporting working. (ii) C1 for a valid comment, e.g. she may get enough tomatoes if each one weighs less than 75 g, but not if it weighs more."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q5",w:898,h:1039,needsHeading:false},n:"5",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Pie charts",marks:6,text:"60 students were asked how they get to school. The table shows the results.\nBus: 15, Walk: 27, Car: 12, Bicycle: 6\n(a) What fraction of the 60 students did not walk to school?\n(b) Complete the pie chart for the information in the table.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 33/60  (b) pie chart completed with correctly sized sectors",markscheme:"(a) M1 for a method to find the number of students who did not walk to school, e.g. 15+12+6, or 60−27 (=33), or 0.55. A1 for 33/60 or an equivalent fraction. (b) M1 for a method to find the angle for at least one sector, e.g. (27/60)×360 (=162°), (12/60)×360 (=72°) or (6/60)×360 (=36°). M1 for drawing at least one sector accurately. A1 for an accurately drawn pie chart. B1 (dependent on all four sectors, at least one accurate) for correctly labelling Walk, Car and Bicycle."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q6",w:980,h:343,needsHeading:false},n:"6",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:2,text:"Annie and Lily share some money in the ratio 4 : 3\n(a) What fraction of the money does Lily get?\nRosie and Dan share some sweets.\nDan gets <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1</span><span class=\"den\">4</span></span> of the sweets.\n(b) Write down the ratio of the number of sweets Rosie gets to the number of sweets Dan gets.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 3/7  (b) 3 : 1",markscheme:"(a) B1 for 3/7 or an equivalent fraction. (b) B1 for 3 : 1 or an equivalent ratio."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q7",w:680,h:148,needsHeading:false},n:"7",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Prime numbers",marks:2,text:"Steve says,\n“There are more prime numbers between 20 and 30 than there are between 10 and 20”\nIs Steve right?\nYou must show how you get your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"No, Steve is not right; both ranges contain two prime numbers",markscheme:"B1 for showing 11, 13, 17, 19 with no non-prime numbers between 10 and 20, or for showing 23, 29 with no non-prime numbers between 20 and 30. C1 (supported) for “No”, supported by listing 11, 13, 17, 19 and 23, 29 and no non-primes."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q8",w:909,h:848,needsHeading:false},n:"8",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Interpreting graphs and charts",marks:2,text:"Chrissy drew this graph to show the percentage of buses that got to a bus stop on time for six months.\n(a) Write down one thing that is wrong with the graph.\n(b) Describe the trend in the percentage of buses that got to the bus stop on time.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) e.g. the vertical scale is not linear (the label 30 is missing between 40 and 20)  (b) The trend is upward / increasing",markscheme:"(a) C1 for a valid statement, e.g. the vertical scale is not linear. (b) C1 for describing the trend, e.g. upward or positive."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q9",w:1045,h:852,needsHeading:false},n:"9",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Bearings and scale drawing",marks:3,text:"Here is a map of an island.\nA straight road joins the two villages, Backley and Cremford.\nScale: 1 cm represents 0.5 km\n(a) Work out the real distance between the two villages.\n(b) Find the bearing of Cremford from Backley.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) in the range 2.65–2.85 km (measurement-dependent)  (b) in the range 128–132° (measurement-dependent)",markscheme:"(a) M1 for accurately measuring the distance between Backley and Cremford as 5.3–5.7 cm, or their measurement × 0.5. A1 for an answer in the range 2.65 to 2.85. (b) B1 for an answer in the range 128 to 132."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q10",w:905,h:903,needsHeading:false},n:"10",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Area of triangles and rectangles",marks:3,text:"The diagram shows two shapes drawn on a centimetre grid.\n(a) Find the area of shape P.\n(b) Write down the mathematical name of quadrilateral Q.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 12 cm²  (b) kite",markscheme:"(a) B1 for the numerical answer 12. B1 for units shown as cm². (b) B1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q11",w:994,h:341,needsHeading:false},n:"11",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:3,text:"The table shows a cricket club’s income in 2016 from a fete, a quiz and membership fees.\nFete: £250\nQuiz: entry fees 13 at £5 each, refreshments £35\nMembership fees: 25 at £20 each\nExpress as a ratio the income from the fete to the income from the quiz to the income from membership fees.\nGive your ratio in its simplest form.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"5 : 2 : 10",markscheme:"P1 for a process to find the total for the quiz or the total membership fees, e.g. 13×5+35 (=100), or 25×20 (=500). P1 for a complete process to write the figures as a ratio, e.g. 250 : 100 : 500 oe. A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q12",w:934,h:647,needsHeading:false},n:"12",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Frequency trees",marks:5,text:"200 people live in a village.\n23 people do not have a garden.\n10 males do not have a garden.\n95 people are male.\n(a) Use this information to complete the frequency tree.\nOne of the people who does not have a garden is chosen at random.\n(b) Write down the probability that this person is female.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) Do not have a garden: 23 (male 10, female 13). Have a garden: 177 (male 85, female 92)  (b) 13/23",markscheme:"(a) C3 for completing all information correctly (C2 for 3 or 4 correct frequencies, or all correct probabilities; C1 for 2 correct frequencies). (b) M1 ft for 13/a (a<23), or b/13 (b>13) oe. A1 ft from (a)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q13",w:798,h:182,needsHeading:false},n:"13",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Rates and unit pricing",marks:3,text:"Ellie makes hats.\nShe makes at least 17 hats per hour.\nShe is paid 46p for each hat she makes.\nReaze is a waiter.\nHe works 35 hours and is paid a total of £266\nShow that Ellie’s hourly rate of pay is more than Reaze’s hourly rate of pay.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Shown: Ellie earns at least £7.82 per hour; Reaze earns £7.60 per hour",markscheme:"M1 for a method started to find comparable amounts, e.g. 17×46 (=782), 17×0.46 (=7.82), 266÷35 (=7.6) or 26600÷35 (=760). M1 for a complete method to find both comparable figures. C1 for showing the correct comparable figures, e.g. 7.82 and 7.60."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q14",w:937,h:329,needsHeading:false},n:"14",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Algebraic proof",marks:4,text:"<em>a</em> and <em>b</em> are odd numbers.\n(a) Give an example to show that the value of 2(<em>a</em> + <em>b</em>) is a multiple of 4\n(b) Show that, when <em>a</em> and <em>b</em> are both odd numbers, the value of 2(<em>a</em> + <em>b</em>) will always be a multiple of 4",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) e.g. a = 1, b = 3: 2(1 + 3) = 8, a multiple of 4  (b) shown",markscheme:"(a) M1 for choosing two odd numbers and substituting into 2(a+b). C1 for calculating 2(a+b) correctly to give a multiple of 4. (b) C1 for stating a+b is even (or 2a is even, or 2b is even). C1 for completing the argument."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q15",w:819,h:280,needsHeading:false},n:"15",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Percentage increase",marks:5,text:"Mr Page uses oil to heat his home.\nAt the beginning of November there were 1000 litres of oil in his oil tank.\nMr Page bought enough oil to fill the tank completely.\nHe paid 50p per litre for this oil.\nHe paid a total amount of £750\nAt the end of February Mr Page had 600 litres of oil in the tank.\nHe bought enough oil to fill the tank completely.\nThe cost of oil had increased by 4%.\nWork out the total amount Mr Page paid for the oil he bought in February.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"£988",markscheme:"P1 for a process to find the amount of oil bought in November, e.g. 750÷0.5 (=1500). P1 for a process to find the amount of oil ordered in February, e.g. “1500”+1000−600 (=1900). P1 (independent) for a process to calculate a 4% increase in price, e.g. 1.04×50 (=52p) or 1.04×750 (=780). P1 for a complete process to find the total cost, e.g. “52”×“1900”÷100, or “780”×“1900”÷“1500”. A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q16",w:819,h:28,needsHeading:false},n:"16",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Solving linear equations",marks:3,text:"Solve 5<em>x</em> − 6 = 3(<em>x</em> − 1)",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"x = 1½",markscheme:"M1 for correct expansion of the bracket, e.g. 3x−3, or dividing all terms by 3 as a first step. M1 for isolating terms in x on one side of the equation, e.g. 5x−6−3x=−3, or both constants on one side, e.g. 5x=3x−3+6. A1 for x = 1½ oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q17",w:1045,h:154,needsHeading:false},n:"17",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Percentage profit and loss",marks:3,text:"Emily buys a pack of 12 bottles of water.\nThe pack costs £5.64\nEmily sells all 12 bottles for 50p each.\nWork out Emily’s percentage profit.\nGive your answer correct to 1 decimal place.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"6.4%",markscheme:"P1 for a strategy to compare the same number of bottles, e.g. £5.64÷12 (=47p), or 12×50p (=£6). P1 for the start of a process to find percentage profit, e.g. 36/564, 3/47 or 6/5.64 oe. A1 for an answer in the range 6.3 to 6.4."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q18",w:1045,h:910,needsHeading:false},n:"18",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Circumference of a circle",marks:3,text:"Hasmeet walks once round a circle with diameter 80 metres.\nThere are 8 points equally spaced on the circumference of the circle.\n(a) Find the distance Hasmeet walks between one point and the next point.\nFour of the points are moved, as shown in the second diagram.\nHasmeet walks once round the circle again.\n(b) Has the mean distance that Hasmeet walks between one point and the next point changed? You must give a reason for your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 31.4 m (accept 10π)  (b) No; the total distance walked (the circumference) is unchanged and there are still 8 gaps, so the mean distance stays the same",markscheme:"(a) P1 for working with the circumference formula, e.g. π×80 (=251.3...). A1 for an answer in the range 31.4 to 31.5, accept 10π. (b) C1 for “No” with a supporting reason, e.g. the mean distance stays the same because the total distance (circumference) is unchanged and there are still the same number of points."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q19",w:703,h:191,needsHeading:false},n:"19",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Probability",subtopic:"Probability from ratio",marks:3,text:"There are only blue cubes, yellow cubes and green cubes in a bag.\nThere are twice as many blue cubes as yellow cubes, and four times as many green cubes as blue cubes.\nHannah takes at random a cube from the bag.\nWork out the probability that Hannah takes a yellow cube.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"1/11",markscheme:"P1 for starting the process, e.g. writing a correct ratio or using given numbers of cubes for one relationship, e.g. B:Y = 2:1 or G:B = 4:1 or G:Y = 8:1 oe. P1 for a complete process to find the ratio of all three colours, e.g. G:B:Y = 8:2:1 oe. A1 for 1/11 oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q20",w:955,h:1028,needsHeading:false},n:"20",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Transformations",marks:2,text:"(a) Rotate trapezium <strong>T</strong> 180° about the origin. Label the new trapezium <strong>A</strong>.\n(b) Translate trapezium <strong>T</strong> by the vector (−1, −3). Label the new trapezium <strong>B</strong>.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) trapezium A correctly plotted  (b) trapezium B correctly plotted",markscheme:"(a) B1 for a correct rotation. (b) B1 for a correct translation."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q21",w:823,h:474,needsHeading:false},n:"21",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Laws of indices",marks:4,text:"3<span class=\"exp\">3</span> × 3<span class=\"exp\"><em>x</em></span> = 3<span class=\"exp\">9</span>\n(a) Find the value of <em>x</em>.\n(7<span class=\"exp\">2</span>)<span class=\"exp\"><em>y</em></span> = 7<span class=\"exp\">10</span>\n(b) Find the value of <em>y</em>.\n100<span class=\"exp\"><em>a</em></span> × 1000<span class=\"exp\"><em>b</em></span> can be written in the form 10<span class=\"exp\"><em>w</em></span>\n(c) Show that <em>w</em> = 2<em>a</em> + 3<em>b</em>",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) x = 6  (b) y = 5  (c) shown",markscheme:"(a) B1 cao. (b) B1 cao. (c) M1 for writing 100^a or 1000^b as a power of 10 (=10^(2a) or 10^(3b)), or 10^(2a+3b), or stating 100=10² and 1000=10³. C1 for a complete chain of reasoning leading to the conclusion."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q22",w:1045,h:323,needsHeading:false},n:"22",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Trigonometry (right-angled triangles)",marks:5,text:"<em>ABCD</em> is a trapezium.\n<em>AB</em> = 7.5 cm, <em>BC</em> = 10 cm, <em>AD</em> = 24 cm.\nThe perpendicular height from <em>BC</em> to <em>AD</em> is 6 cm.\nWork out the size of angle <em>CDA</em>.\nGive your answer correct to 1 decimal place.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"32.3°",markscheme:"P1 for using Pythagoras to find the length of the third side of the right-angled triangle, e.g. 7.5²−6², or uses trigonometry to find an angle, e.g. sin A = 6/7.5. P1 for a complete process to find that length, e.g. √(7.5²−6²) (=4.5). P1 for 24−10−“4.5” (=9.5). P1 (independent) for a process to find angle CDA, e.g. tan CDA = 6÷(base). A1 for an answer in the range 32.2 to 32.3."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q23",w:652,h:316,needsHeading:false},n:"23",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Using a calculator",marks:3,text:"Use your calculator to work out\n√<span class=\"radicand\"><span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">sin 25° + sin 40°</span><span class=\"den\">cos 25° − cos 40°</span></span></span>\n(a) Write down all the figures on your calculator display.\n(b) Write your answer to part (a) correct to 2 decimal places.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 2.7560609...  (b) 2.76",markscheme:"(a) M1 for 1.0654(059...), 0.1402(633...) or 7.5957(541...) seen, or 2.756 truncated or rounded to no fewer than 2 dp. A1 for 2.7560(...). (b) B1 for 2.76, follow through from (a)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-2F-Q24",w:460,h:501,needsHeading:false},n:"24",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Quadratic expressions and equations",marks:5,text:"(a) Solve 2<em>x</em>² = 72\n(b) Expand and simplify (2<em>x</em> + 1)(3<em>x</em> − 2)\n(c) Factorise <em>x</em>² + 6<em>x</em> + 9",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"2",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) x = ±6  (b) 6x² − x − 2  (c) (x + 3)²",markscheme:"(a) M1 for one value (6 or −6), or √36, or an embedded answer, e.g. 2×6²=72. A1 for ±6. (b) M1 for at least 3 of the 4 terms correct from the expansion (or all 4 correct ignoring signs). A1 cao. (c) B1 for (x + 3)² or (x + 3)(x + 3)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q1",w:433,h:23,needsHeading:false},n:"1",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Rounding and decimal places",marks:1,text:"Write 3758 correct to the nearest 1000",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"4000",markscheme:"B1 for 4000."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q2",w:311,h:28,needsHeading:false},n:"2",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Simplifying and collecting terms",marks:1,text:"Simplify <em>y</em> + 3<em>y</em> − 2<em>y</em>",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"2y",markscheme:"B1 for 2y."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q3",w:370,h:23,needsHeading:false},n:"3",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Multiples and factors",marks:2,text:"Write down all the factors of 18",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18",markscheme:"B2 for all 6 factors with no incorrect values (B1 for at least 3 factors with no more than one error)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q4",w:846,h:626,needsHeading:false},n:"4",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Money and time calculations",marks:5,text:"The table gives information about the prices of cinema tickets.\nAdult ticket: £7.80. Child ticket: £5.80. Family ticket (for 4 people): £24.30\nMr Edwards and his 3 children go to the cinema.\nIt is cheaper for Mr Edwards to buy 1 family ticket rather than 4 separate tickets.\n(a) How much cheaper?\nThe film starts at 6.45 pm.\nThe film lasts 102 minutes.\n(b) What time does the film finish?",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 90p  (b) 8.27 pm",markscheme:"(a) M1 for a correct first step from which a complete method could be developed, e.g. 5.80×3 (=17.40), or 24.30−7.80 (=16.50). M1 for a complete method, e.g. 7.80+5.80×3−24.30 (=0.90). A1 for the answer in correct notation with correct units, e.g. 90p or £0.90 (SC B1 for an answer of £2.90). (b) M1 for using 60 minutes = 1 hour in the conversion of 102 minutes, e.g. 1 h 42 mins, or (60+42) mins, or 102−60, or 102÷60. A1 for 8.27(pm) oe."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q5",w:894,h:154,needsHeading:false},n:"5",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Calculations with measures",marks:3,text:"Thais has a large bottle of shampoo.\nThere are 2 litres of shampoo in the large bottle.\nThais also has some empty small bottles.\nEach small bottle can be completely filled with 150 ml of shampoo.\nHow many small bottles can be completely filled with shampoo from the large bottle?",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"13",markscheme:"M1 for the start of a method, e.g. 2×1000 (=2000), or 150÷1000 (=0.15), or 1000÷150 (=6.66...). M1 for a fully correct method, e.g. 2000÷150. A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q6",w:961,h:607,needsHeading:false},n:"6",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Pictograms",marks:3,text:"The incomplete pictogram shows information about the number of cycles sold in a shop on Tuesday, on Wednesday and on Thursday.\nA total of 20 cycles were sold on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.\n8 cycles were sold on Friday.\n15 cycles were sold on Saturday.\nUse this information to complete the pictogram.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Friday: 2 whole circles. Saturday: 3¾ circles (key: 1 circle represents 4 cycles)",markscheme:"C1 for deducing that one circle represents 4 cycles (20÷5), or that ½ circle represents 2 cycles, or ¼ circle represents 1 cycle. C1 for 2 circles drawn for Friday. C1 for a fully correct pictogram, including key."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q7",w:764,h:411,needsHeading:false},n:"7",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Geometric proof",marks:4,text:"<em>BCD</em> is a straight line.\n<em>ABC</em> is a triangle.\nAngle <em>ABC</em> = 54°. The exterior angle at <em>C</em> (angle <em>ACD</em>) = 117°.\nShow that triangle <em>ABC</em> is an isosceles triangle.\nGive a reason for each stage of your working.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Triangle ABC is isosceles (angle BCA = angle CAB = 63°, shown with reasons)",markscheme:"M1 for angle BCA = 180−117 (=63). M1 for angle CAB = 180−“63”−54 (=63), or angle CAB = 117−54 (=63). C2 for a statement, e.g. isosceles since angle BCA = angle CAB = 63 with fully correct reasons, from: angles on a straight line add up to 180°; angles in a triangle add up to 180°; the exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the interior opposite angles (C1 for angle BCA = 63 and angle CAB = 63 with one correct reason)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q8",w:1045,h:479,needsHeading:false},n:"8",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Estimation and scale reading",marks:2,text:"The picture shows a bus next to a building.\nThe bus has a length of 12 m.\nThe bus and the building are drawn to the same scale.\nWork out an estimate for the height, in metres, of the building.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"in the range 27–33 m (measurement-dependent)",markscheme:"M1 for 12 m = 1.9 to 2 cm, or for a scale factor of 2.25 to 2.75 (comparing the length of the bus with the height of the building), or a complete method using the height of the bus to compare with the height of the building. A1 for an answer in the range 27 to 33."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q9",w:928,h:126,needsHeading:false},n:"9",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Prime numbers",marks:2,text:"Nidah writes down two different prime numbers.\nShe adds together her two numbers.\nHer answer is a square number less than 30\nFind two prime numbers that Nidah could have written down.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"2 and 7, or 3 and 13, or 5 and 11, or 2 and 23",markscheme:"M1 for identifying two different prime numbers or two numbers which add to give a square number, or for a list of at least 3 prime numbers with no errors and a list of 3 square numbers with no errors. A1 for two correct prime numbers."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q10",w:348,h:150,needsHeading:false},n:"10",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Number",subtopic:"Fractions of amounts",marks:2,text:"Jim thinks of a number.\n<span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">2</span><span class=\"den\">3</span></span> of Jim’s number is 48\nWork out <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">5</span><span class=\"den\">6</span></span> of Jim’s number.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"60",markscheme:"M1 for a method to find the number, e.g. 48×(3/2) (=72), or to find 1/6 of the number, e.g. 48÷4 (=12). A1 cao."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q11",w:907,h:337,needsHeading:false},n:"11",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Percentage decrease (discounts)",marks:3,text:"Jack’s driving school has two offers.\nOffer 1: first driving lesson free, all other lessons normal price.\nOffer 2: all driving lessons 5% off the normal price.\nThe normal price of a driving lesson is £24\nDouglas is going to have 12 driving lessons.\nWhich is the cheaper offer for 12 driving lessons, Offer 1 or Offer 2?\nYou must show how you get your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Offer 1 (£264, compared to £273.60 for Offer 2)",markscheme:"P1 for a process to find the cost of 12 lessons under Offer 1, e.g. 24×(12−1) (=264), or for a process to find 5% (or 95%) of an appropriate amount, e.g. 24×0.05 (=1.20) or 24×0.95 (=22.80), for Offer 2. P1 (supported) for a complete process leading to values for comparison, e.g. 264 and 24×0.95×12 (=273.60). C1 for “Offer 1” with correct comparative values."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q12",w:815,h:63,needsHeading:false},n:"12",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Direct and inverse proportion",marks:2,text:"2.5 kg of apples cost £3.60\nWork out the cost of 3.5 kg of apples.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"£5.04",markscheme:"M1 for a correct first step to find the cost of a unit weight, e.g. 3.60÷2.5 (=1.44), or a complete alternative method. A1 for 5.04 (accept £5.04)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q13",w:911,h:1096,needsHeading:false},n:"13",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Straight-line graphs",marks:5,text:"(a) Complete the table of values for <em>y</em> = <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1</span><span class=\"den\">2</span></span><em>x</em> − 1\n(b) On the grid, draw the graph of <em>y</em> = <span class=\"frac\"><span class=\"num\">1</span><span class=\"den\">2</span></span><em>x</em> − 1 for values of <em>x</em> from −2 to 3\n(c) Use your graph to find the value of <em>x</em> when <em>y</em> = 0.3",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) x: −2,−1.5,−1,−0.5,0,0.5 for y = −2,−1.75,−1.5,−1.25,−1,−0.75 (accept table values consistent with the line)  (b) correct straight line drawn  (c) in the range 2.5–2.7",markscheme:"(a) B2 for a fully correct table (B1 for 2 or 3 correct entries). (b) M1 for correctly plotting at least 5 points (provided the table is correct), or for a straight line with gradient 0.5, or for a straight line through (0,−1) with a positive gradient. A1 for a correct line between x = −2 and x = 3. (c) B1 for an answer in the range 2.5 to 2.7, or follow through from a single straight line with positive gradient."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q14",w:786,h:589,needsHeading:false},n:"14",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Transformations",marks:2,text:"Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape <em>A</em> onto shape <em>B</em>.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Reflection in the x-axis (y = 0)",markscheme:"B1 for reflection. B1 for the x-axis (or y = 0). No marks awarded if more than one transformation is given."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q15",w:981,h:464,needsHeading:false},n:"15",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Direct and inverse proportion",marks:3,text:"The ratio of the cost of one metre of cotton fabric to the cost of one metre of silk fabric is 2 : 5\nComplete the table of costs for 2 m, 6 m, 8 m and 9 m of each fabric.\nCotton fabric costs £6 for 2 m.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"Cotton: £6, £18, £24, £27. Silk: £15, £45, £60, £67.50",markscheme:"M1 for a proportional method to find at least one cost for cotton, e.g. £6÷2×9 (=£27), or a correct table entry. M1 for a proportional method to find at least one cost for silk, e.g. £6÷2×5 (=£15), or a correct table entry. A1 for a fully correct table (accept 67.5(0))."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q16",w:1045,h:910,needsHeading:false},n:"16",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Surface area and volume",marks:5,text:"Chloe has a van. She is going to use the van to deliver boxes.\nEach box is a cuboid, 40 cm by 30 cm by 35 cm.\nThe space for boxes in the van has maximum length 2.4 m, maximum width 1.5 m and maximum height 1.4 m.\nThe space for boxes is empty.\nChloe wants to put as many boxes as possible into the van.\nShe can put 3 boxes into the van in one minute.\nAssume that the space for boxes is in the shape of a cuboid.\n(a) Work out how many minutes it should take Chloe to put as many boxes as possible into the van.\nThe space for boxes might not be in the shape of a cuboid.\n(b) Explain how this could affect the time it would take Chloe to put as many boxes as possible into the van.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 40 minutes  (b) e.g. it could take more time, since a different arrangement would be required, or less time if fewer boxes fit",markscheme:"(a) P1 for the start of a process to find the number of boxes that fit along one edge, e.g. 240÷40 (=6), 150÷30 (=5) or 140÷35 (=4), or for a process to find a volume, e.g. 40×30×35 (=42000). P1 for a complete process to find the maximum number of boxes, e.g. “6”×“5”×“4” (=120). P1 (dep) for (their number of boxes) ÷3, e.g. 120÷3 (=40). A1 cao. (b) C1 for an explanation with an appropriate reason, e.g. less space means fewer boxes fit, taking less time, or a different arrangement would take more time."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q17",w:824,h:327,needsHeading:false},n:"17",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Factorising and algebraic vocabulary",marks:3,text:"(a) Factorise 4<em>m</em> + 12\n(b) Choose two words from expression, equation, formula, identity, inequality, term, factor, multiple to make this statement correct:\n5<em>y</em> is a ...................... in the ...................... 3<em>x</em> + 5<em>y</em>",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 4(m + 3)  (b) term, expression",markscheme:"(a) B1 for 4(m + 3) or 2(2m + 6). (b) B1 for ‘term’ in the first space. B1 for ‘expression’ in the second space."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q18",w:891,h:392,needsHeading:false},n:"18",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Algebra",subtopic:"Sequences (nth term)",marks:4,text:"Here is a sequence of patterns made with counters.\n(a) Find an expression, in terms of <em>n</em>, for the number of counters in pattern number <em>n</em>.\nBayo has 90 counters.\n(b) Can Bayo make a pattern in this sequence using all 90 of his counters? You must show how you get your answer.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 3n + 1  (b) No",markscheme:"(a) M1 for a method to deduce the nth term, e.g. 3n + k where k is a constant, or n = 3n + 1. A1 for 3n + 1 oe. (b) C1 for using their expression from (a) equal to 90, or showing that 88 or 91 is in the sequence. C1 for an answer of “No” with a convincing argument, e.g. pattern number 30 has 91 counters, or (90−1)÷3 (=29.66...)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q19",w:854,h:947,needsHeading:false},n:"19",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Statistics",subtopic:"Frequency polygons and grouped data",marks:3,text:"The table shows information about the heights of 80 children.\nHeight (h cm): 130 < h ≤ 140 (freq 4), 140 < h ≤ 150 (freq 11), 150 < h ≤ 160 (freq 24), 160 < h ≤ 170 (freq 22), 170 < h ≤ 180 (freq 19)\n(a) Find the class interval that contains the median.\n(b) Draw a frequency polygon for the information in the table.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"(a) 150 < h ≤ 160  (b) frequency polygon plotted at interval midpoints and joined with line segments",markscheme:"(a) B1 for the correct class interval. (b) C2 for a fully correct frequency polygon: line segments joining the points (135,4), (145,11), (155,24), (165,22) and (175,19) (C1 for points plotted correctly at midpoints, or for line segments at the correct heights within intervals, or for a correct polygon with one point incorrect)."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q20",w:728,h:178,needsHeading:false},n:"20",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Currency and unit conversion",marks:3,text:"In London, 1 litre of petrol costs 108.9p\nIn New York, 1 US gallon of petrol costs $2.83\n1 US gallon = 3.785 litres\n£1 = $1.46\nIn which city is petrol better value for money, London or New York?\nYou must show your working.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"New York",markscheme:"P1 for changing between £ and $, e.g. 1.089×1.46 (=$1.589), or between litres and gallons, e.g. 1.089×3.785 (=$4.121). P1 for a complete process to give comparable values, e.g. “1.589”÷3.785 (=$0.512 per litre), or 2.83÷1.46 (=£1.938 per gallon) then ÷3.785 (=£0.512 per litre). C1 for “New York” with correct comparative values."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q21",w:1045,h:126,needsHeading:false},n:"21",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Geometry and measures",subtopic:"Density, mass and volume",marks:3,text:"A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg.\nThe density of gold is 19.3 g/cm³\nWork out the volume of the gold bar.\nGive your answer correct to 3 significant figures.",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"648 cm³",markscheme:"M2 for a complete method, e.g. 12.5×1000÷19.3 (M1 for using volume = mass÷density, e.g. 12500÷19.3, condoning inconsistent units). A1 for an answer in the range 647 to 648."},
{qimg:{src:"Nov2017-3F-Q22",w:768,h:161,needsHeading:false},n:"22",tier:"Foundation",strand:"Ratio, proportion and rates of change",subtopic:"Ratio problems",marks:3,text:"There are only blue pens, green pens and red pens in a box.\nThe ratio of the number of blue pens to the number of green pens is 2 : 5\nThe ratio of the number of green pens to the number of red pens is 4 : 1\nThere are less than 100 pens in the box.\nWhat is the greatest possible number of red pens in the box?",paper:"Papers 2 & 3 (calculator)",paperNum:"3",sitting:"November 2017",answer:"15",markscheme:"P1 for a strategy to combine the ratios, e.g. 8:20 and 20:5. P1 for a process to solve the problem, e.g. finding the combined ratio 24:60:15 (blue:green:red) and scaling to stay under 100 pens. A1 cao."},
